articles.title: gamescom Apologizes for Its Initial Response to Thefts, Promises Improved Security Measures
articles.summary: gamescom has provided a second response regarding the theft of developers’ equipment during its event, offering an apology for its initial reaction to the ordeal.
articles.body:
gamescom has provided a second response regarding the theft of developers’ equipment during its event, offering an apology for its initial reaction to the ordeal.

On August 28, 2026, indie developer Ryan Laley uploaded a video to X/Twitter claiming that all of his laptops had been stolen at gamescom. He wasn’t the only one affected; several other developers spoke out with similar stories, saying their equipment had also been pilfered at the event.

gamescom responded to the ordeal on August 29, writing that while it was "very sad" about the situation, it "would like to inform [attendees] about general security regulations."

My #gamescom cut short. Our equipment was stolen last night from the booth. Police reports have been filed. At a loss for words to describe the feeling. Just defeated. Gonna do my best with what's left of the week. But a huge blow financially and mentally pic.twitter.com/dKpp3Of6df — Mimic | Ryan Laley (@RyanLaley) August 28, 2026

My #gamescom cut short. Our equipment was stolen last night from the booth. Police reports have been filed. At a loss for words to describe the feeling. Just defeated. Gonna do my best with what's left of the week. But a huge blow financially and mentally pic.twitter.com/dKpp3Of6df

"Individual stand security can be booked separately, and exhibitors are advised to insure equipment against theft. This is noted in the terms and conditions of participation and the technical guidelines," it said. "...At an event of this size, however, there will always be individuals attempting to take advantage of the situation. Our security measures are designed to minimize such risks as effectively as possible.”

This statement didn’t go over well. A swath of fellow exhibitors, attendees, and onlookers online felt that gamescom’s reply placed blame on victims of the theft, slamming the event for its "unacceptable response."

Today, September 4, gamescom posted a follow-up statement on social media, in which it apologized for its initial post. It also announced plans to improve security moving forward, promising to host a roundtable discussion with developers who had indie booths at the event.

You can read the statement in full below:

"Over the past few days, we have received a great deal of criticism for the way we communicated about the theft of hardware belonging to several indie developers. That criticism is justified. Our first response did not strike the right tone, and it did not show the people affected the empathy they deserved. We are sorry. A theft like this is far more than a material loss. It can ruin an entire gamescom for the people it happens to, and it can destroy work that took months or years to build - work that, for a small studio, can be almost everything.

"To everyone affected: we understand what this has cost you, and we should have said so from the very first moment. We have already begun talking with those affected - about the theft, about its consequences, and above all to listen. We have also been moved by how this industry responded. Within hours, people offered help - unconditionally, and without being asked. That says a great deal about this community, and we are grateful for it. What it does not do is relieve us, as the organizers, of our own responsibility to work together with our exhibitors and partners to create the best possible environment for everyone.

"We are therefore committed to jointly reviewing and further improving security. Here is what we are doing: Alongside our regular post-event review and our evaluation of exhibitor feedback, we will carry out a dedicated review of security for indie exhibitors. In the coming weeks, we will invite organizers of shared indie booths to a roundtable, so that we can develop concrete measures together.

"We also urge every exhibitor who has experienced an incident to report it - to us and to the police - even if it happened some time ago. Only then can incidents be documented, possible connections between them investigated, and appropriate action taken. You can reach us at sales@gamescom.de . gamescom is made by the industry, for the industry. It lives on the passion of the people who build it, and that includes the many small studios who matter to us enormously. Our commitment has always been to keep making gamescom better - together with the community, not just when things go well. That is exactly what we will do here. Thank you to everyone who is helping us."

Luckily, several good Samaritans have stepped in to help the developers affected by the thefts in the aftermath. Most notably, The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077 developer CD Projekt Red reached out to Laley on social media, promising to "send a few things" his way. Don’t Scream dev Joe Henson, AKA Indie Game Joe, also offered to help out, transforming a tragic situation into a heartwarming show of support and community effort.

articles.title: 'No One Puts Double Fine Out of Business Except for Me' — Tim Schafer Explains How He Kept Double Fine Afloat After Leaving Xbox
articles.summary: Tim Schafer, game designer and founder of Psychonauts developer Double Fine, gave a strong response after Xbox divested the studio as part of its massive restructuring efforts this summer.
articles.body:
Tim Schafer, game designer and founder of Psychonauts developer Double Fine, gave a strong response after Xbox divested the studio as part of its massive restructuring efforts this summer.

Speaking with Bloomberg's Jason Schreier in a September 2026 interview , Schafer admitted that he knew something was up before Xbox’s divestment was officially announced — but he wasn’t about to go down without a fight.

"You’re like, 'Wait a second, we’re not going out like this,'" Schafer explained. "Some people said, 'I’m checking out, this is one too many battles for me.’ But for the rest of us, it’s like a creative awakening."

"No one puts Double Fine out of business except for me," he continued. "Asha’s not going to shoot my dog. I’m going to shoot it. But I’m not going to shoot it, because it’s going to do great. A lot of people want to walk the dog."

Thankfully, Double Fine was able to retain its intellectual property and become fully independent, though it did have to lay off a quarter of its staff as a result of this change. That isn’t stopping it from making more games, though, as the developer recently published a Kickstarter for its next project — with the addendum that if it raises $100 million, they’ll also make Brutal Legend 2.

"We’ve been through a lot this year," Schafer told Schreier. "A lot of it is very soul-sucking stuff. Inner conflict, threats of extermination, long negotiations, strenuous hard tradeoffs with lawyers. Tons of demoralizing stuff."

And yet, in spite of these challenges, Schafer says he’s been able to find a creative spark that has invigorated both himself and the remaining team at Double Fine.

"This is the good fight. Can we think of a great idea for a game that we can actually do for the right budget, that can get to this publisher who’s interested in these types of games? This kind of problem-solving is soul-enriching. Using creativity to solve problems is what gets us up in the morning. So it is hard, and it is scary and it is stressful, but it’s at least putting some fire back into the bellies of the team and me," he said.

Xbox has undergone a slew of major changes as CEO Asha Sharma works to make the company profitable again. Shedding Double Fine was part of that change, as well as massive layoffs that affected roughly 3,200 employees.

Sharma has been fairly transparent with Xbox’s financial state and future plans, most recently telling the BBC that the brand’s next generation console, Project Helix, will include a “family of devices,” though she notably declined to comment if it’ll have a disc drive or not.

In other Double Fine news, the developer shadow dropped Keeper , a formerly Xbox-exclusive title, on PlayStation 5 today now that it's no longer tied to the company.

articles.title: 14 Predictions for the September 2026 Nintendo Direct and Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct
articles.summary: IGN's Logan Plant shares 14 predictions for the pair of Nintendo Directs airing in the coming days.
articles.body:
Nintendo is hosting two Directs in the coming days , and it’s pretty much all I’ve been thinking about since the announcement. On Tuesday, September 8, it’s The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct, followed by a more general Nintendo Direct on Wednesday, September 9. While we wait, it's predictions time!

Before we start, a couple of disclaimers: these are all purely my guesses based on public information and my analysis of Nintendo’s release patterns, and nothing more. Nothing here is based on any inside information. But, I will be discussing a couple of relevant leaks over the last few months, so if you have been steering clear of information like that, you may not want to read on.

Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct Predictions

Zelda is my favorite series, so I’m buzzing thinking about all the possibilities we could see Tuesday morning. But I’m trying to keep things realistic in this piece and only sharing predictions that I think have a legitimate chance of happening.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Full Reveal

This will undoubtedly be the centerpiece of the presentation. We’ve only seen a few seconds of footage of the Ocarina of Time remake , which is set to come out in 2026. So, now’s the time for the full reveal trailer and release date. I can’t wait for this one; my imagination has been running wild over this remake for the last three months, and we’re finally going to see more about the scope of this remake. Is it faithful, or more of a reimagining? What does the kingdom of Hyrule look like beyond Link’s treehouse? All that and more will likely be answered by a more conventional trailer that gives us a proper look at the remake.

I don’t know exactly what Ocarina of Time will look like, but the teaser trailer from earlier this year tells me Nintendo is very confident in this game. You don’t set the internet’s imagination on fire with a 10-second tease of Link’s treehouse if you don’t have really satisfying answers to share when you do finally pull the curtain back, and I expect the Ocarina of Time remake to be a pretty big deal.

As for a release date, I’m expecting Ocarina of Time to arrive on Thursday, November 12. Nintendo doesn’t have a game dated for November yet (Fire Emblem arrives this month, with Nintendo Switch Sports slated for October), and it never misses putting out a big game in the weeks before Black Friday. Knowing it’s coming this year, Zelda feels primed for that spot. Nintendo is extremely unlikely to release a game on Thanksgiving (that’s Thursday, November 26 in the U.S.), and it has no reason to go head-to-head with Grand Theft Auto VI on November 19. That just leaves November 5 and 12 as available Thursdays to launch a game. A few weeks back, the Nintendo UK store briefly dated a couple of Kirby Air Riders amiibo for November 12 , and Nintendo typically launches amiibo the same day as a first-party game, even if the franchises aren’t related. That date has since been removed, but I’m still pretty locked in on November 12 as Ocarina of Time’s release date.

With amiibo on the mind, I’m hopeful we’ll get a glimpse of a new amiibo line for Ocarina of Time alongside the reveal. Zelda games typically get tie-in amiibo figures (Echoes of Wisdom is a rare recent exception), so I’m expecting we’ll see figures of Young Link and Adult Link at the very least.

Special Edition Nintendo Switch 2 and Pro Controller

A few weeks ago, allegedly leaked designs surfaced for a Zelda-themed Nintendo Switch 2 console and Pro Controller. These don’t appear to be branded for Ocarina of Time specifically, but rather for the 40th anniversary as a whole. If they’re legitimate, it'd make the most sense to see the products formally announced on Tuesday, potentially alongside my predicted November 12 release for Ocarina of Time. And if they don’t show up, you can pretty confidently write that leak off as fake. Right now, my gut says they’re real and will show up.

The Legend of Zelda movie hits theaters next April, and aside from casting news and a few official teaser images from Nintendo, we haven’t seen anything from the film. It’s become common for Shigeru Miyamoto to show up to present Mario movie news in Directs, so it seems very likely that he’ll do the same here. I think we could get official casting news for Ganondorf and other characters that have been reported on in recent weeks, and I bet we’ll see a short clip, too, if not a full trailer.

In June, Nintendo unveiled the DK Challenge: a series of time-limited challenges tied to Donkey Kong Bananza and classic DK games available on Nintendo Switch Online. It’s Nintendo’s experimental take on achievements or trophies, and notably, the DK Challenge just ended earlier this week. Based on the way it was integrated into Switch 2’s OS, this concept doesn’t seem like a one-off, and I can’t think of a better choice to follow it up than holding the Zelda Challenge for the franchise’s 40th anniversary. I’m not sure what modern game would be tied into this – maybe Breath of the Wild? – but this seems like a good way to build hype for the milestone year while encouraging fans to revisit classic Zeldas in the weeks leading up to Ocarina of Time.

Twilight Princess on Nintendo Switch Online

Speaking of NSO, it bothers me more than it should that The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess is the only 3D Zelda game that’s not playable in some form on Switch 2. Its excellent soundtrack isn’t available on the Nintendo Music app either, which strikes me as odd. I think Nintendo will right both of these wrongs on Tuesday, by shadowdropping the GameCube version of Twilight Princess on Nintendo Switch Online and adding its music to the app shortly after. Twilight Princess turns 20 years old in just a couple of months, so now seems like the perfect time.

The Zelda Direct is 30 minutes long, so I think there’s time for one more game announcement in addition to everything I’ve already discussed. If I’m putting this presentation together, though, I don’t really want to overshadow Ocarina of Time with anything too big. With that said, I think the time is right for the return of a multiplayer Zelda game. Nintendo hasn’t put out a multiplayer-focused Zelda game since 2015’s Tri Force Heroes on 3DS, and neither it nor the Four Swords games are available on Switch or Switch 2.

It’s a more niche corner of the franchise that’s been neglected for some time, and there are a few ways a multiplayer surprise could go down. We could get the “Zelda 99” battle royale treatment we’ve seen applied to classic games like Tetris, F-Zero, Pac-Man, and even Super Mario Bros. for its 35th anniversary. Or, it could be an NSO rerelease of the Game Boy Advance’s Four Swords, or the GameCube’s Four Swords Adventures, either of which could hugely benefit from online multiplayer support. Of course, it could be a brand new game in the style of past co-op Zeldas, but that feels the least likely. No matter what form it takes, I’m ready to see multiplayer Zelda return in the Direct.

The core 3D Zelda team – led by Director Hidemaro Fujibayashi and longtime series producer Eiji Aonuma – are no doubt hard at work on their followup to 2023’s Tears of the Kingdom. The question is, will we see it on Tuesday? I’m inclined to guess we won’t. Ocarina of Time is the big Zelda story right now, and even a glimpse of what’s next might take away from the conversation surrounding the remake. If it does show, though, I don’t think it’d be any more than the smallest of teases. We’re talking five to 10 seconds of Link looking over a hill. But I’m not holding my breath. Especially with another general Nintendo Direct the following day, there’s no need to fire the open-world Zelda cannon at this point in the Switch 2’s life.

My Pie-in-the-Sky Dream: The 8-bit Breath of the Wild Prototype Is Released

I said all of my predictions were meant to have a solid chance of happening, but this one’s just for me. While exploring early concepts that would lead to the development of Breath of the Wild, the Zelda team built a playable, 8-bit prototype to test their ideas. It demonstrated ideas like chopping down trees to cross rivers and fire spreading across a grassy field, set in a Hyrule reminiscent of the NES original. It wasn’t meant to be a commercial product, but how cool would it be if Nintendo dropped it on Switch as part of the anniversary celebrations? I think the odds of this happening are essentially zero, but I’d love nothing more than to have access to a playable piece of Breath of the Wild’s development history.

That’s just day one! On Wednesday, September 9, Nintendo is airing its general Direct, featuring 45 minutes of updates on Nintendo Switch 2 games. This one is particularly exciting for different reasons: the Zelda Direct is presumably all about getting answers to our Ocarina of Time questions, while we have no idea what the centerpiece of the Wednesday show will be.

Much of the runtime will likely go to final updates and trailers on Nintendo games still set to come out this year. Expect last looks at Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave (out September 17) and Nintendo Switch Sports Resort (October 22), as well as updates on Pokémon Pokopia’s next waves of DLC.

We could also get another look at Xenoblade Genesis, Monolith Soft’s next RPG that’s due out in 2027. Something I’m not expecting to see is Pokémon Winds & Waves , though. It’s also set for next year, but given that mainline Pokémon games typically release in the Fall, I’m not expecting to see the next generation show up again until a Pokémon Presents showcase in February 2027 at the earliest.

Following its network test last month, I think we’ll get a release date for FromSoftware’s The Duskbloods. The Nintendo Store still lists it as a 2026 game, and December is feeling the most likely to me right now. Nintendo is publishing The Duskbloods outside of Japan. If you follow the pattern of Nintendo typically publishing one game a month, and you accept my reasoning that Ocarina is the November game, the only month left for The Duskbloods to theoretically land in is December. Purely to get a guess on the record, I’ll predict Thursday, December 3, mostly for the reason that when Nintendo does publish a game in December, it’s generally pretty early in the month, like Metroid Prime 4: Beyond on December 4 last year.

On the topic of Metroid, it’s time to see MercurySteam’s next entry in the 2D Metroid series. The studio released Samus Returns on 3DS in 2017 and Dread on Switch in 2021, so it feels like we’re due for a new one in 2027. There was a recent video game age rating leak out of Brazil for a submission titled “Metroid Ravenous” . That leak featured no details other than the name, so there’s still a lot up in the air. However, Dread’s main villain was named Raven Beak, making “Ravenous” a pretty intriguing title for a potential sequel. Nintendo has been revealing new games fairly close to their release dates over the last few years, so I wouldn’t be surprised to see Metroid Ravenous announced on Wednesday and released as early as Q1 of 2027.

There’s been this itch in the back of my brain all day. Nintendo has never aired back-to-back Directs in this way on two consecutive days. In other years, they’ve just glued the Mario 40th Anniversary segment onto a larger Nintendo Direct. I find the order peculiar, too. If the Zelda Direct blows us away (which I’m expecting Ocarina of Time to), why isn’t that one airing second as the big endcap to the week? Ocarina of Time has the power to close out a show, but it’s probably not going to be a factor on Wednesday. This tells me Nintendo must have something pretty special to end its second Direct with. Something big that won’t launch until the second half of 2027, but the announcement alone will help fuel Switch 2 sales through the holiday season. The two things I can think of that fit the bill are either Super Smash Bros. or the next 3D Super Mario. I think we’ll see one – not both – of these announced at the end of Wednesday’s show.

I can see arguments for each: I predicted a Super Smash Bros. Ultimate - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition at the start of the year. Here’s what I said in January that I still feel today:

“My boldest call of them all is that we’ll get a tease this year for Super Smash Bros. Ultimate - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition to launch sometime in 2027. I believe Ultimate could get the Mario Kart 8 Deluxe treatment this generation, with an enhanced port that carries us through the next several years rather than an entirely new entry. Smash Bros. director Masahiro Sakurai wrapped up Kirby Air Riders a few months ago, and it’s entirely possible he’s already hard at work bringing Ultimate over to Switch 2 with a few new characters. Ultimate noticeably hasn’t received a Switch 2 performance patch like Super Mario Odyssey, the open-world Zeldas, and plenty of other best-selling Switch 1 games, and combined with the fact that a new Smash game almost always hits within the first two years of a new Nintendo console, it feels like a prime candidate for a Switch 2 Edition.”

And, after spending the last year declaring it to be too soon for 3D Mario in the wake of Donkey Kong Bananza – another 3D mascot platformer from much of the same team as 3D Mario – I now think we’re entering the window where we could see the plumber show up any time. The Bananza marketing cycle is winding down: the DK Challenge just ended on NSO, the Emerald Rush DLC has gone through an entire year of limited-time events, and by the time 2027 rolls around, Bananza will have had two full holiday seasons as the primary platformer on Switch 2. I think Mario’s time is coming.

This is one of my favorite series, and I predict it every time. It has to happen at some point!

Those are my predictions for the pair of Nintendo Directs airing over the next few days. I can’t wait to cover it all here on IGN and Nintendo Voice Chat. Be sure to drop your own predictions in the comments!

Logan Plant is the host of Nintendo Voice Chat and IGN's Senior Editor, Playlist and DB. The Legend of Zelda is his favorite video game franchise of all time, and he is patiently awaiting the day Nintendo announces a brand new F-Zero. You can find new episodes of NVC every Friday on the IGN Games YouTube channel, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app.

articles.title: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis Could Be Great, But There's Some Things We Can't Ignore...
articles.summary: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis shows massive potential, but controversial changes like skill trees and modern hand-holding threaten to frustrate fans. And some of that food looks very suspicious.
articles.body:
The first thing that strikes you upon seeing the new Tomb Raider live-demoed on a massive 115” TV mere inches from your face, I can attest, is its visual fidelity: Legacy of Atlantis is absurdly pretty. Crammed with fine detail enough that every particle of dust and bat guano flitting through the stale air poses danger to your airways, it almost feels like it’s supposed to be funny when compared to the chunky textures and pointy polygons of the 32-bit original.

The game’s director Raul Siqueira puts it nicely during our session: “the secret to a good remake is knowing what to change, and what to leave well alone”. Absolutely. Preserving the essence of a thing is much more vital than slavishly recreating the original work, and this is certainly something that Legacy of Atlantis understands, aesthetically at least. It is unmistakably a modern interpretation of Lara Croft’s seminal adventure, an essential piece of gaming history arguably as important as Super Mario Bros . or Chuckie Egg (ask your dad).

This latest preview focuses on LoA’s interpretation of the Damocles Room, the infamous chamber of raining swords that caused instant death for the uncareful while sifting through the tombs of ancient Greece. It’s a frighteningly vertical space, one that cemented Tomb Raider’s reputation for traversal-puzzles and terrifying jumps that make your insides curdle. Legacy of Atlantis preserves these aspects and then some, the feeling of being a tiny speck of human in an impossibly deep cavern of flakey pillars and dusty godrays made all the more potent by the sheer graphical prowess on offer. That fine detail, that premium fidelity, it stretches off into the distance and pulls off a sense of scale that could only be hinted at on PS1 hardware. Or PS2 hardware. Or PS3, for that matter.

And these swords that dangle so menacingly, they’re big. They’re almost house-sized.. The big twist in this version of the Damocles Room is that, rather than being deadly obstacles, the swords are helpful almost to the point of politeness: they’re needed for traversing the space, as Lara can now perch on their hilts after they’ve dropped. And in stark contrast to bat poop, the dropping itself barely poses any danger. The swords are easily dodged, and their drops can be triggered from a safe distance by shooting at them, rendering them little more than another minor inconvenience that Lara gets to solve with hot lead.

Much like the poor leopard she encounters on the way here, on which the camera lingers majestically as she delivers a breathless “magnificent” right before shooting it in the face. I thought this was hilarious and burst out laughing involuntarily, which turned out to be massively out of step with the rest of the room. I even asked the devs about this in the following Q&A: “Is that meant to be funny?”

No, basically. While Lara has no shortage of handy quips, delivered with requisite English public-school plummyness by the wonderful Alix Wilton Regan, this is I’m assured a serious game with a serious tone. So anyone expecting a modicum of self-awareness from this third distinct version of Lara’s original adventure, not counting the recent remaster, will be disappointed.

It highlights a tonal mismatch between the various eras of Lara Croft that this game seeks to blend together. As a nexus point of Crystal Dynamics’ new “unified timeline” for the series, Legacy of Atlantis seeks to replace both the original game and 2007’s Anniversary in the PS1 and Legend timelines, while serving as a sequel to the Survivor Trilogy, which we last visited in 2018’s Shadow of the Tomb Raider . It requires a lot of mental gymnastics to imagine that all of these disparate Laras are the very same bored aristocrat, not least because each of them reflects the time they were conceived in. It’s clear that neither the original games nor the Legend timeline are occurring after the mid-2010s, as clear as it is that this new take on Lara’s original adventure isn’t happening in 1996.

You could argue that it’s all supposed to feel timeless and perpetual, like The Simpsons, but you can’t tell me that pointy PS1 Lara Croft looks like she knows what an iPhone is. There’s also an element of parody to the previous eras, as plenty of Indiana Jones and sixties spy tropes were playfully redeployed as foils for 90s Girl Power, and then again as welcome ballast to the prevailing dourness of post-9/11 Bond movies. A playfulness that the Survivor Trilogy dropped entirely, focusing sharply on the 2010s appropriate misery of being a teenager who unwittingly spends her gap year having to murder dozens of Russian mercenaries while worrying about whether her tetanus shots are up to date.

The point is, all of these flavours of Tomb Raider are distinctly of their time, which is absolutely fine. Smooshing them together into a paste is a weird decision and one that seems to be inspiring some questionable choices, like the inclusion of survival mechanics like crafting and skill trees in this redux of Lara’s original adventure, things that seem to be there just because the last game had them or, worse, because that’s what games are like now. Things that don’t make thematic sense: if this is 2013 Lara finally reaching her prime, her zenith, her most capable self – as the survivor trilogy always promised to be leading to – then why are we still spending the game unlocking her skills?

Why are we “surviving” at all, eating foraged meals cooked in the field, when this isn’t a survival scenario? Lara hasn’t been stranded here, she came to these ruins of her own accord, presumably in a rented jeep. It’s only Greece, you can go on Ryanair for twenty quid. This is a capable explorer who would have a meticulous itinerary and a bag full of protein bars and jerky, she wouldn’t be winging it on the basis of eating boiled moss.

Nor would this classically educated aristocrat seem to need a detective mode scanner thing that gives her puzzle hints and provides handy historical commentary. In fairness, its usage is entirely optional, and seems to be there to address a common criticism of the more recent Tomb Raiders, namely that Lara seems to spend a lot of time chatting to herself.

None of these things are dealbreakers, they’re just prominently questionable choices in a game full of them. As is the decision to employ, then defend, the studio’s use of generative AI in development. Granted, feelings in the community are mixed on this – some care, some don’t, most are probably blissfully unaware of the controversy – but it tends to go down like a shotgunned leopard with enthusiasts, and so using it at all feels like unnecessarily tainting your project before it’s even out.

Because they’ve admitted to using it, it’s hard not to look for evidence of it. I’ll be blunt, the food crafting menus are looking very suspicious. Video game depictions of food are an art form in and of themselves, and often, they are notable for looking absolutely delicious. Who can forget the sweetrolls of Skyrim or the lavish gourmet meals conjured up by Ignis in Final Fantasy 15? In Legacy of Atlantis, though, the food looks kinda disgusting. Despite what the accompanying description says, Lara’s lunches all look rather aptly like slop. Mushy stews of unrecognisable plant matter and meat you’d hesitate to put in a dog.

To be clear, this is all circumstantial – we don’t know for sure if these elements are derived from AI, and the studio for their part has insisted that everything in the final game will be human made or human “refined” – but it demonstrates how damning even a faint association with generative AI can be. Especially if the results are this unappetising.

The game is still many months away from release, and what we’ve seen of it so far is by no means final. There’s time to iron out the kinks and excise the final traces of generative AI that may or may not be plaguing the current build (not that you can un-use genAI any more than a bat can un-shit a temple floor).

As the second remake of a ground-breaking game, Legacy of Atlantis has a lot to live up to. It certainly justifies itself by playing differently from the existing versions: there’s never been a Tomb Raider game quite like this, for better or worse. And though the challenge element has been dramatically reduced in the Damocles Room (and therefore, one presumes, the rest of the adventure), incorporating the giant swords into a traversal puzzle is inspired, and the way it plays out in the demo hints at something fresh: a puzzle with a fixed solution, but multiple routes to reach it.

And it really can’t be stressed enough how beautiful it all is. On a technical level the fidelity in every image is positively retina-searing, but it’s all sumptuously lit and pocked with a gnarly decay that makes the ancient world sing with a sense of history. Lara herself has never looked better, a depiction that successfully blends the slightly cartoony Lara of the Legend trilogy with her naturalistic, mud-caked, cortisol-saturated counterpart of Tomb Raider 2013. New Lara spent her youth avoiding certain death in some of the most deadly corners of the earth, from Syria to Siberia, yet moves with all the balletic flourishes that the Survivor Trilogy sidelined in favour of Uncharted-style handhold grappling. Every jump, flip, and bullet-time whip exudes joy: this is a Lara who revels in being Lara. She even does that handstand backflip thing when hoisting herself onto a platform (in the build we saw, a little too often, but I heavily suspect it was dialled up for this demo).

There’s a lot to love here. A celebration of all Tomb Raiders past and present, one that treats all of the previous eras as equally important to the series’ legacy, is refreshingly inclusive. In these sorts of franchise overhauls, someone’s favourite usually gets overlooked in pursuit of whatever is deemed to be the most iconic or fundamental. To have a project here that treats the whole thing as gospel is admirable, if dauntingly hard to chew.

As someone who grew up with Lara and has enjoyed every iteration of Tomb Raider, I desperately want to be on board for this new, unified journey. But a mixture of dubious choices, mechanical and ethical, are making it a tough sell at the moment. I very much doubt Lara would choose to consume suspicious looking slop if any alternatives were available, and neither should anyone else.

Jim Trinca is a Video Producer at IGN, and when he isn't fawning over Assassin's Creed, he can be found watching Star Trek and eating stuff. Follow him on @jimtrinca.bsky.social , and check out The Trinca Perspective playlist over on IGN's YouTube channel!

articles.title: South Park, A Different World, and 8 More of Our Most Anticipated Streaming Shows and Movies in September
articles.summary: From a Reacher spin-off to a return to Hillman College and the Season 4 finale of Strange New Worlds, here are our picks for what to stream this month.
articles.body:
It’s back-to-school time, and you know what that means: It’s back to your TV screens as well to decompress after a long day of book learnin’. And lucky you, there’s a ton of great TV (and movies) coming to streaming this month for September 2026, so let’s break down some of the highlights.

Fan of Prime Video’s Reacher? While the fourth season of the series is ending this month (and there’s a fifth in the works), you’ve also got a brand new spin-off dropping all in the same day to enjoy. How about space stuff? Strange New Worlds is ending with an intriguing sounding finale that sets up the final season of that series. And if you prefer comedies or true crime? We’ve got that too.

Okay, enough set-up — let’s get into the list. Here are our 10 most anticipated shows and movies streaming in September. And don’t forget, kids: Study hard and stay in school… or watch TV, do whatever you want.

(Note: This list is presented in release date order.)

Ryan Reynolds pretty much doesn’t miss and Kenneth Branagh is a reliable star as well. But the biggest selling point for this throwback action adventure on Apple TV? Writers and directors Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley. While they wrote Spider-Man: Homecoming, the real sell here is that they’re the team behind the superb Game Night, the transcendently hilarious Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, and the highly underrated but also hilarious Vacation remake.

With Mayday , the duo take on the sort of Cold War comedies that pervaded the ’80s — think Spies Like Us — as Reynolds plays an American pilot crash-landed in Soviet Russia, forced to team up with an ex-KGB/America aficionado played by Branagh who wants to defect to the good ol’ US of A. It’s an across-the-plate premise that in lesser hands might be the umpteenth disposable action movie on a streaming service this month, but in the hands of Goldstein and Daley, you know this is gonna get weirder and wilder than expected. (Read our Mayday review .)

A lot of all-timer comedies took the first season to figure themselves out. Think The Office, Parks & Recreation; even Brooklyn Nine-Nine had to spend several episodes hashing out the character dynamics and rhythms. So will Peacock’s The Paper be the same?

The first season had a great cast, including Domhnall Gleeson as Ned, the eternally optimistic new Editor-in-Chief of the Toledo Truth Teller running a staff of mostly zero-experience news writers while clashing with the digital-first Esmerelda (Sabrina Impacciatore) and sparking a “will-they won’t-they” romance with the only good news reporter, Mare (Chelsea Frei). But it mostly couldn’t quite figure out what it wanted to be until the excellent final episode of the season.

So will the presses be running for The Paper Season 2? The good news (you get it) is this is an Office spin-off, so it’s got a great model to work from when it comes to the second season of a series. Ensembles take time, comedy takes time, and here’s hoping the Toledo Truth Teller has the ink to make a stink in Season 2… by which we mean, “get people talking.” That’s what that meant. (Read our The Paper Season 2 review .)

The best spy show on TV is back for the next yearly installment of six episodes on Apple TV, which definitely isn’t enough… but we’ll take what we can get. Starring Gary Oldman as the disgusting, farting head of Slough House — basically where MI5 sticks the spies they don’t want anymore — the latest season is based on two of Mick Herron’s novels: Joe Country and Slough House.

The headline for this season of Slow Horses is a new showrunner. Show creator Will Smith departed with Season 5, and Gaby Chiappe took over as head writer (Ben Vanstone is taking over for Season 7, which will likely debut next year). Don’t worry, though; Chiappe is a pro, having written dozens of episodes of TV since 1997 as well as several films.

And beyond Oldman, the rest of the cast is back too, with Kristin Scott Thomas’s Diana Taverner finally First Desk (aka head of MI5) and Jack Lowden’s River Cartwright dealing with a devastating loss. There’s also the return of a few familiar faces (no spoilers here, though Apple put one of the big spoilers right in the trailer). The show is funny and smart with some great action and excellent character dynamics, so trot over to your TV and get caught up for Slow Horses Season 6 right now.

What is there to be said about South Park , the nearly 30-year-old animated series, at this point that we don’t already know? It’s ostensibly about a bunch of kids living in the small town of South Park, Colorado, but really, it’s a chance for creators/billionaires Trey Parker and Matt Stone to say whatever they want about society and the US government in particular.

So what will happen in the upcoming 29th season? Pick up a newspaper or click on over to your fave news website (IGN of course), and whatever is a hot button issue this week will surely make it onto the series later in the week. After a renewed cultural relevance with Season 28 and a contentious upcoming midterms election, chances are that Parker and Stone will go for the jugular once again.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story (September 17)

Despite frequent accusations of front-loading the killers and diminishing the stories of victims, Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s monster (sorry) hit Netflix anthology is back with a new installment. In a resounding girl boss move, it’s turning the lens to female killers; heck yeah — you go girl!

Specifically, the show is focusing on famous axe murderer Lizzie Borden, who reportedly gave her mother forty whacks and then her father forty-one. But this will likely be a more grounded version of the classic nursery rhyme, featuring an as-usual-for-a-Murphy-production all-star cast: Ella Beatty (previously of Murphy’s Feud) stars as Lizzie Borden alongside Charlie Hunnam, Rebecca Hall, Sarah Paulson, Billie Lourd, and more.

At the very least, moving the action to 1892 should probably make it harder for any of Borden’s victims’ families to complain versus previous seasons of Monster. But hey, we haven’t encountered a Murphy production yet that didn’t cross a line somewhere!

Not to be confused with 2009’s Brothers (starring Jake Gyllenhaal and Tobey Maguire), 2024’s Brothers (starring Josh Brolin and Peter Dinklage), or Brothers from 1977, 2004, 2023, or the other Brothers from 2009 (starring Michael Strahan and Carl Weathers), Brothers stars Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey in the roles they were born to play: Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey.

The Apple TV series pivots on how everyone always joked they were like brothers, then continued to joke about that when they were on True Detective, and then discovered via a dive into their family history that they may indeed be half-brothers. Maybe. What Brothers (2026) presupposes is: What if they were brothers? The show takes a metafictional approach to that narrative, with the duo playing semi-fictionalized versions of themselves.

Confused? Don’t be, as the show is essentially Yellowstone but with Harrelson and McConaughey trying to unravel their (fictional) shared family history. Alright? Alright. Alright.

The hierarchy of power in the Reacher Cinematic Universe is about to change. The same day that the fourth season of the Large Man Series wraps up on Prime Video, the streamer will launch spin-off Neagley , which front-loads Maria Sten’s title character as she investigates a mystery of her own.

Unlike the fathership show, which rolls out semi-weekly episodes, Neagley will premiere all episodes on the same day… so just like Reacher himself, you’ll have an oversized nine hours of TV to watch (the Reacher Season 4 finale plus eight episodes of Neagley).

Alongside Sten, the show also stars Adeline Rudolph and Greyston Holt, with Alan Ritchson guest-starring as Reacher for Maximum Spinoff Potential.

Strange New Worlds Season Finale – “Tomorrow’s Enterprise” (September 24)

While the fourth season of Paramount+’s Star Trek: Strange New Worlds has mostly been done-in-one adventures, the season finale has an extremely intriguing title, particularly given Season 5 will be an abbreviated final season of the series: “Tomorrow’s Enterprise.”

Even without context, those words could make your ears perk up higher than Spock’s (Ethan Peck) as the well-received prequel series heads towards the end/beginning, with Captain Kirk (Paul Wesley) taking over from Captain Pike (Ethan Peck). So certainly this title could merely refer to the eventuality of the events of the Original Series picking up where Strange New Worlds leaves off.

But! The Next Generation episode “Yesterday’s Enterprise” found the crew of the Enterprise-D encountering the presumed destroyed Enterprise-C thanks to what is scientifically known as “shenanigans.” The Next Gen folks ended up changing time by the end of that episode to save yesterday’s Enterprise; could a similar scenario play out in this upcoming Strange New Worlds episode? Could Kirk’s Enterprise end up back in time, encountering Pike’s Enterprise and showing them a glimpse of the future (something an intrepid, probably time-traveling Reddit user called four years ago )?

Or even more intriguingly; What if we skip Kirk entirely and go all the way forward to the Enterprise-G as seen at the end of Picard Season 3, captained by Seven of Nine (Jeri Ryan)?

Adding fuel to any of these theories: September 8 is the official 60th anniversary of Star Trek. While this episode doesn’t quite line up, what better way to pay tribute to the franchise than with the current flagship show meeting the future… quite literally?

A different world ? Not more multiverse stuff. Do we really have to do — oh wait, we’re being told this is actually a revival of the iconic sitcom/spinoff of The Cosby Show, now back as a legacy sequel with returning and new cast.

Set at Hillman College (an HBCU), the daughter of the original series’ Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison) heads into her first year only to find herself living in the shadow of her parents’ legacy while also trying to find time to balance studies, partying, and likely social issues (a la the purview of the original).

The big difference? While episodes are still half an hour-ish, this is a single camera comedy and not a three-camera comedy like the OG sitcom. Still, it’ll include plenty of the original cast members making their return from the groundbreaking series 39 years later.

If you’re Netflix and looking to dramatize the life of the Unabomber , aka Ted Kaczynski, the natural choice is — of course — child star Jacob Tremblay.

We’re joking, but Tremblay has been a standout ever since his award-winning performance in Room. Now 19, he’ll play the infamous serial bomber in two timelines — one set during the manhunt that tried to track him down, and one during his time at Harvard University leading up to his stint as the mysterious hooded, sunglasses-wearing criminal.

While this is far from the first time the events surrounding Kaczynski have been dramatized, this movie does sport a great cast including Russell Crowe, Shailene Woodley, Annabelle Wallis, Steven Ogg, and more. It’s directed by Janus Metz Pedersen, who also directed three episodes of Andor Season 2 — the episode leading to, including, and dealing with the fallout from the Ghorman Massacre — to give you a sense of what might be in store.

Will you be watching any of these this month? What else are you looking forward to that we didn’t get to? Vote in our poll and let’s discuss in the comments!

You can chat with Alex Zalben on BlueSky @azalben.bsky.social , or find him regularly yapping on the Comic Book Club podcast .

articles.title: Is the Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM Worth Its $1,199 Price Tag? We Tested Its 4K/240Hz and 1080p/480Hz Dual-Mode Performance to See if It’s the Ultimate Gaming Monitor.
articles.summary: The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM offers a gorgeous display that works as well for cinematic games as it does for competitive, fast-paced ones.
articles.body:
Asus already had one of IGN’s favorite 4K gaming monitors on its hands with the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP , delivering a gorgeous OLED panel that could render 4K games at a zippy 240Hz or swap to 1080p for an even faster 480Hz. It’s still an excellent option on the market and made all the more affordable by its age. Now almost two years on, Asus has the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM, a very similar monitor with a smaller 27-inch panel that gets some new display tech for slight visual refinement. Of course, newer tends to mean more expensive, and this model is set to come in at $1,199, putting it well ahead of other competing OLED displays like the earlier PG32UCDP, which was sitting at $859 at the time of writing, or the 1440p/500Hz MSI MAG 272QP QD-OLED X50 at $599. Let’s have a look at how it stacks up.

Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM – Hands-on Photos

Asus didn’t leave much out when it designed the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM. That said, it doesn’t have speakers, but you’ll find it checks boxes in just about every other department.

From the front, it looks like a fairly tame, cleanly-built gaming monitor with perhaps a bit of a gaudy stand thanks to the angular, gamery aesthetic and the LED bat signal of the ROG logo that it wants to splash onto your desktop day and night (this can be turned off, thankfully). If you want, you can swap for a VESA stand using an included adapter. The provided stand is plenty functional, though, offering the typical range of adjustments you’ll find on a high-end monitor. There’s also a slot in the neck of the stand for passing through cables, and where some monitor stands make it quite a squeeze to even get power and a single HDMI cable through this portal, the PG27UCWM provides plenty of room for multiple cables.

The PG27UCWM is ready for a lot of cables, too. You’ll find two HDMI 2.1 ports, a DisplayPort 2.1a port, and even a capable USB-C port that’ll take in video and send out up to 90 watts of power. There are two USB ports for passing data to a connected system, letting the monitor serve as a USB hub as well with a KVM switch so you can pass that connection to the USB-C link or a separate USB-B link. If you want to connect speakers, there’s a headphone jack, too.

Around back, the PG27UCWM spices things up a little. Rather than the classic black ABS plastic you’ll find on half the monitors in the world, the PG27UCWM opts for a transparent plastic that gives it something of a cyberpunk aesthetic. It may still feel like cheap plastic, but it looks damn good.

Another feature is a presence sensor that can help preserve the lifespan of the OLED panel by dimming it whenever you step away. I didn’t find it overly sensitive, so I wasn’t concerned it’d blink off while I’m in the middle of a game.

Adjusting settings in the monitor is easy with a joystick control for navigating menus and making selections. This sits just behind the presence sensor at the bottom edge of the display.

Then there’s the display itself. The ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM packs a 4K/240Hz display with HDR10 and Dolby Vision support, variable refresh rates down to 48Hz, and a setting that swaps the display to 1080p and cranks the max refresh rate up to 480Hz.

The display is glossy, which can hurt in a bright room, but it has a decent anti-reflection coating that at least cuts down on how bright reflections appear.

The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM proves its worth with strong performance in objective measurements. My colorimeter measured a wide color gamut with 100% coverage of sRGB, 89% coverage of AdobeRGB, and 97% coverage of DCI-P3 color spaces. The monitor delivers the color accurately with an average dE1976 of 1.04 and a max of 2.66, making this a solid option for creative work. The monitor achieved these results in its default Racing picture profile, but not all different settings will perform as well. The Scenery picture profile, for instance, had a bad color accuracy dE1976 average of over 10.

By default, the display ran a tame 147.6 nits that would be comfortable in a modestly lit room, and that comes alongside infinite contrast thanks to 0.0-nit black levels. This level came alongside a standard 2.2 gamma curve and a comfortable 6600K whitepoint. Bumping the brightness level to 100% raised the white level to 249.7 nits.

HDR is a specialty for this display. It may not go incredibly bright for a full screen in normal use, but it can bring out more light in HDR. I measured a 294.8-nit whitepoint for a full screen and a 519-nit whitepoint for a 10% window with the remaining screenspace blacked out. That could go higher still for smaller highlights, but required switching the monitor to its Adjustable HDR setting and raising the brightness to 100%. In those conditions, I measured a 4% window at 1,066 nits and a 1% window at 1,172 nits. Those high brightness levels can sag quickly, but for temporary, bright bursts of HDR highlights, they’ll dazzle.

Motion clarity is also exceptional. The monitor's support for a 240Hz refresh rate in 4K or 480Hz in 1080p combined with the ultra-fast pixel response time of OLED keeps details sharp in fast motion.

The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM’s panel is excellent for both work and play. OLED panels had already been shifting away from troublesome sub-pixel layouts that could show color fringing on fine detail and text or basically anywhere with a sharp edge. With the PG27UCWM, Asus incorporates a panel with an RGB strip sub-pixel arrangement, aligning with the sub-pixel arrangement of your typical monitors and thus avoiding the issue entirely. Working in text documents, watching movies, and playing games, I never spotted the color fringing that had impacted some earlier OLED display.

Even if it had the fringing, it might have been hard to spot since the 4K panel is stunningly sharp on a 27-inch screen. I didn’t find myself pixel peeping. The screen looks great for movies, which are sharp and really play up the contrast and color the panel can provide. If you pair the monitor with the right video source, you can even tap into Dolby Vision.

Gaming just makes things all the better. Getting to run at up to 240Hz even at 4K makes the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM quite the sight, and for more competitive or fast-paced games, the option to drop down to 1080p and crank it up to 480Hz can come in clutch. I played through a chunk of Assassin’s Creed Shadows and enjoyed the sharp detail and potent contrast that brings the game world to life one day, and the next swapped over to 1080p so I could blitz through levels in Hades 2 and power through enemies in Trepang2. The monitor kept up with all the intense action and kept the details incredibly clear.

Switching modes is also simple. A single tap on a dedicated shortcut button switches between modes (a clear on-screen indicator of this happening would be helpful, though).

The 1080p resolution starts to hurt a little on the 27-inch panel, but you really only need to swap over when you are playing something that calls for more than 240fps, and in those cases, the pixels will generally be moving too fast to notice them individually.

articles.title: King and Queen join Highland games fans at Braemar Gathering
articles.summary: The King and Queen watched events including Highland dancing, caber tossing and pipe bands performing at the annual event in Royal Deeside.
articles.body:
King Charles and Queen Camilla have joined cheering crowds watching Highland games events at the annual Braemar Gathering in Royal Deeside.

The event, which draws spectators from around the world, is held on the first Saturday of September every year and coincides with the monarch's annual summer holiday at nearby Balmoral.

Among the events watched by the spectators were tug-of-war, caber tossing, hammer throwing, Highland dancing and a parade of pipe bands.

This is the third Games that the King has attended since his coronation.

As he always does when staying in Scotland, the King wore a kilt - which he first unveiled on Burns Night last year .

It is made from the King Charles III tartan, based on the Balmoral tartan sett - or pattern - which dates back to about 1850.

Meanwhile Queen Camilla also dressed in tartan, paired with the emerald green jacket and feathered hat she wore to a Sunday service at Crathie Kirk last year.

Braemar has hosted the Games in its current form for nearly 200 years.

Queen Victoria attended in 1848 and since then, it has been attended regularly by the reigning monarch.

articles.title: Bruce Campbell Says He Has 5 Years Left to Live Amid Cancer Battle
articles.summary: Evil Dead star Bruce Campbell said he has just five years left to live amid his ongoing battle with cancer.
articles.body:
Evil Dead star Bruce Campbell said he has just five years left to live amid his ongoing battle with cancer.

The legendary horror actor gave fans an update on his health during an appearance on The Adam Carolla Show earlier this week. He explained his cancer diagnosis is something that is "treatable" but "not curable."

"In my world, I'm in a five-year prognosis," Campbell said. "The type of cancer I have, which I don't want to get into, the current thing is a five-year deal."

The show's host then asked the 68-year-old actor for clarification, questioning if that meant he had five years left to live.

The actor announced his cancer diagnosis in March of this year, confirming that convention appearances and work in general would "take a back seat to treatment." He added at the time that he was "a tough old son-of-a-bitch" and that he expected "to be around for a while."

During the new interview, Campbell admitted there are plenty of stories of others fighting cancer who outlive their initial timelines, adding that medical technology could become more advanced during his own fight. For him, though, the real battle is "to live with it, not die from it."

"You can go down a massive rabbit hole," he continued. "The cancer rabbit hole is enormous. You can go into focus groups of 10,000 guys who have the exact thing you have. I won't touch it with a 10-foot pole."

He added, "They say there's a whole mental component. You start getting all this bad news, and you're starting breakfast with a s**t sandwich with a side of what-the-f**k for a couple of months as it all comes in. Then, you deal with it, and you have to make this decision of, 'OK, but do I have to stop everything that I'm doing because of this?' Well, no."

Campbell is currently promoting his new film, Ernie & Emma, which he directed, wrote, and starred in. It follows a man who sets out on a journey to spread his wife's ashes following her death. The movie's official tagline is as follows: "'Til death do us part – and a little longer."

"I crack up at the people who are the 'How old can I get? How can I change my lifestyle so I live the longest?'" Campbell said earlier in the new interview. "It's funny; the more people obsess about that crap, I'm like, 'You're not really living. You just have a new hobby that you're obsessing over.' What is the quality of these extra years? So, you get five more years – so what are you doing with those five years? Obsessing about the five years, or are you actually doing something?"

Campbell also addressed his situation with a follow-up post on X/Twitter . In the post, he said, "Cancer is all the rage, but I've said plenty and I need to get back to the business of living." He also recently confirmed he will not return to play his long-running Evil Dead character, Ash Williams .

articles.title: How to Navigate Rebecca Yarros' Popular Fourth Wing Book Series
articles.body:
Rebecca Yarros has been writing romance novels for more than a decade now , but it's her popular romantasy series that has truly caught fire. Fourth Wing, the first book in the Empyrean series, is a spicy story about a dragon academy and magic. Thanks to a massive surge in fans, the series has quickly become one of the most popular new stories in recent memory. There's even an Amazon TV series in the works for it already and multiple board game adaptations.

If you're new to the Empyrean series or romantasy in general, starting with Fourth Wing is an excellent choice. Rebecca Yarros is also coming out with a companion book this year called Threshing Day , which takes place across different points in the book timeline.

There are a ton of different ways to enjoy books these days, and the Empyrean series is available in pretty much every format. If you don't care about reading physical books, I'd suggest checking out the Kindle versions first. The Fourth Wing books absolutely dominated the Kindle charts last year with the release of Onyx Storm, and reading digitally is by far the most convenient way to enjoy the story. That being said, the paperback and hardcover editions are similarly priced.

If you prefer to listen to audiobooks, the original version narrated by Rebecca Soler has received rather mixed reviews online. For the best possible experience, you'll want to check out the dramatized adaptations of the first book. These feature a full cast and offer a much richer experience.

Fourth Wing, The Graphic Novel: Volume One (The Empyrean Series)

The Fourth Wing series is getting its first graphic novel next year, which was recently announced with a release date of April 6, 2027. The cover art has yet to be revealed, but the listing states that it will be 256 pages long and adapts chapters 1-22 of the first book. Yarros has also mentioned that she's already written the second graphic novel , so the next volume is in the works.

Where Does Threshing Day Fit on the Empyrean Timeline?

Threshing Day (Wing and Claw Collection) (The Empyrean)

Rebecca Yarros is releasing a new novel in the series this month, but this one is a bit different. Threshing Day is a collection of short stories about various characters' Threshing Day. While we get a look at Violet Sorrengail's Threshing Day via Fourth Wing, this new book is about seeing some other key perspectives on the day they bonded with their dragons.

As for where these stories actually fit on the timeline, it depends on which characters are featured. We've gotten confirmation that Xaden's story is included in the collection, which took place a couple of years before Violet joined Basgiath War College. If other older characters like Brennan and Mira are also featured, the book will be jumping to various points in the past.

Rebecca Yarros has been fairly busy working on projects that aren't the fourth book in the Empyren series. Because of that, we still don't have any concrete details about when we should expect the next novel to be announced. Based on her previous releases and writing schedules, fans have speculated that we could get a new novel as early as 2027. Without any official announcements from Yarros herself, it's impossible to pin down when to expect the next direct sequel.

Jacob Kienlen is a Senior Audience Development Strategist and Writer for IGN. Born and raised in Portland, Oregon, he has considered the Northwest his home for his entire life. With a bachelor's degree in communication and 10 years of professional writing experience, his expertise is spread across a variety of different pop culture topics -- from TV series to books and the latest LEGO sets .

articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Passes 1 Million Copies Sold in Just 2 Days
articles.summary: Single-player RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold 1 million copies just two days after its launch, publisher Bandai Namco and developer Rebel Wolves have announced.
articles.body:
Single-player RPG and new IP The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold 1 million copies just two days after its launch, publisher Bandai Namco and developer Rebel Wolves have announced.

Official social media accounts for the first-time developer's new game confirmed the news with a celebratory graphic today. The milestone was reached just 48 hours after The Blood of Dawnwalker launched for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S September 3.

"Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community!" Rebel Wolves said in a message to fans.

Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community! ❤ pic.twitter.com/9fNqO8gNGB — Dawnwalker (@DawnwalkerGame) September 5, 2026

Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community! ❤ pic.twitter.com/9fNqO8gNGB

An official summary for The Blood of Dawnwalker describes it as an "open-world dark fantasy action RPG set in 14th-century Europe." In this first chapter, players take the role of Coen, a "human by day and vampire by night" who is fighting for his family in a narrative shaped by player choice. It also happens to have an in-game clock that sees Coen's story take place through a 30-day period . It's something some players love – and others don't .

Reaching 1 million copies sold in such a short amount of time would be an impressive feat for any game, but there are a few reasons it's especially noteworthy for the Rebel Wolves team. This is the studio's first major release since it was founded in 2022 . Led by The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt director and Cyberpunk 2077 co-director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, The Blood of Dawnwalker is also a new IP. The Warsaw-based studio previously released a CGI teaser to tease how sequels could potentially expand on its dark fantasy formula in new and interesting ways.

"The CGI teaser shows where the dark fantasy saga is heading," Bandai Namco said in a June press release. "Players can see Coen in completely different surroundings than the ones they are used to – a modern, 21st-century setting, offering a glimpse of where the overarching plot ultimately leads. As the developers revealed, the next installments of the Dawnwalker franchise will span centuries, continents, and cultures across the globe."

Surreal. Thank you so much!🔥🙏 — Mateusz Tomaszkiewicz 🧛‍♂️ (@MTomaszkiewicz) September 5, 2026

Speechless. Proud. Tearing up a little 🥹 We're a passionate bunch. And we're not stopping here 😤 Thank you for trusting us ❤️ — Paweł BANAN Panasiuk 🍌 (@pawpanasiuk) September 5, 2026

Speechless. Proud. Tearing up a little 🥹 We're a passionate bunch. And we're not stopping here 😤 Thank you for trusting us ❤️

Tomaszkiewicz said at the time that each installment in the Dawnwalker series is planned to be a standalone entry "with its own story, without narrative cliffhangers, unresolved plot threads, or time travel ideas." With 1 million copies in players' hands out of the gate, those sequels already feel more likely to materialize. Although the when and where for these planned follow-ups have yet to be revealed, narrative director Jakub Szamałek has at least told fans to keep an eye out for "breadcrumbs related to the overarching plot spanning the saga" in The Blood of Dawnwalker.

It helps that Rebel Wolves secured solid reviews upon the launch of its first game. IGN, for example, called it "amazing" in our 9/10 review . We said, "The Blood of Dawnwalker is an impressive, bloody cocktail of interesting ideas and well-written characters, making it one of this year’s best open-world RPGs."

We'll have to wait to see what updates Bandai Namco and Rebel Wolves have in store. In the meantime, you can read what Tomaszkiewicz had to tell us when it comes to the studio's plans to establish even more new IP . For everything you need to know before starting the game yourself, click here .

articles.title: Robert Pattinson's Primetime Is a Blast From the Past With a Sickly Allure, and as Garish as Its Subject, Chris Hansen’s To Catch a Predator
articles.summary: A blast from the past with a sickly allure, the Robert Pattinson romp Primetime is as garish as its subject: Chris Hansen’s To Catch a Predator.
articles.body:
This review is based on a screening from the Venice Film Festival. Primetime is in theaters on September 25.

You don’t have to be familiar with Chris Hansen or To Catch a Predator to enjoy Primetime — director Lance Oppenheim’s feature debut — but it certainly helps. That’s not because the movie sticks closely to real events, but rather, because it takes some audacious swings while purposefully fudging the timeline. Watching exactly how and why it takes these liberties is a delight of its own; the result is a sleazy, rollicking, razor-wire drama that’s every bit about the rise of reality TV as it is a spiritual part of it. Anything is fair game if it makes for a good story.

It begins with TV personality Hansen (Robert Pattinson) privately repeating sexually explicit chat logs sent from a skeevy former Marine (Tony Revolori) to a fictitious adolescent. As he rehearses to ambush the unsuspecting perv — the premise of his hit sting operation, which ran from 2004 to 2007 — the movie starts to reveal its lurid flourishes. Awash in shadow, its heightened version of Hansen is a cartoonishly sinister figure who steps before the cameras with all the boastful poise of a Broadway veteran. When he finally reveals himself to Revolori — after gazing at him through a crack in a door, like some stalker or slasher villain — he towers over the former soldier like a hunter cornering prey.

As his show rises through the ranks, NBC executives make eager demands — Bigger! Flashier! More! — which leads Hansen and his team to more opportunistically (and more voraciously) pursue potential perps, eventually chasing someone they suspect of having a position of influence. Those in the know will recognize this throughline as that of the series’ botched episode emanating from Murphy, Texas, and the subject of the incredible long-form Esquire piece on which Primetime was based. However, en route to that tragic debacle, the movie takes incredibly entertaining turns, buoyed by a raucous visual energy while remaining rooted in surprisingly cogent drama.

The film has no qualms about its culprits’ misdeeds, but it makes sure to frame Hansen and, well, almost everyone involved with the show as some kind of seducer too, whether through its visual framing or its cast’s creepy physicality. A magnetic Merritt Wever plays Hansen’s fictitious producer Andie Bender, whose polite tone disguises exploitative commands, while Matthew Maher portrays the real Xavier Von Erk, the keyboard warrior enthusiastically ensnaring potential perps. Rounding out the sting crew are the experienced, conscientious adult decoy Del (Phoebe Bridgers), a self-professed activist who has the bait-and-switch process of welcoming child predators down pat, and nubile newcomer Dan Plum (Skyler Gisondo) — based loosely on Dan Schrack — a wannabe actor out to prove himself and join the Screen Actors Guild.

Gisondo is the movie’s naïve heart and soul. While initially unaware of the job he agrees to, Dan is eager to please his bosses, especially the imposing Hansen, with whom he forms a perverse father-son dynamic. All Dan wants is approval, but Hansen’s attention is always elsewhere, either on trying to up his TV ratings, or on retaining the illusion of domestic bliss with his wife and sons, while he’s either out philandering — a later development in Hansen’s life brought forward for the movie — or worse, making money off garish spectacle.

The real Hansen hasn’t seen the film at the time of this writing, though this hasn’t stopped him from threatening legal action. Regardless, it’s hard to imagine he’d be pleased with Pattinson’s portrayal — but unfortunately, he might be alone in his displeasure. The Batman star has never been better or more explosive, delivering a jester-like performance as a man envious of other news hosts’ success — and by proxy, of the era of war-as-entertainment. Pattinson smuggles, beneath the character’s wholesome poise, a petulant, paranoid man with a distinctly rehearsed quality. That he nails Hansen’s voice is a fantastic party trick, but this is, quite fittingly, the only truly Hansen-esque thing about him. He’s Chris Hansen in name and occupation; in spirit, he’s an impish embodiment of Hollywood id at the turn of the century, a TV landscape defined by façade, and the willingness to step on anyone to get ahead.

Driven enough to believe his own hype, Hansen commands the movie’s breakneck unfurling as the sickly centerpiece of several rapid montages and a palette that’s both oversaturated and has too much contrast for comfort. Its sensory re-creation of cheap, mid-2000s video recordings makes it especially eerie, as though Primetime were a version of a events we were never meant to see — made all the more haunting by Hansen’s strange segues into fictitious Indian folklore, meant to build himself up as some spiritual savior.

The dialogue and its double meanings are incredibly on-the-nose — what Hansen says, versus what he means deep down, is a disconnect apparent to everyone but him — resulting in some jaw-dropping hilarity. While there’s certainly a wider discussion to be had about the show’s methods and its modern legacy, this conversation is already underway courtesy of the aforementioned Esquire piece, as well as David Osit’s 2025 documentary Predators, an intimate retrospective on the series.

Primetime, on the other hand, is a macabre, poetic echo of the temptations To Catch a Predator first tapped into. Its public pillorying led to plenty of cases that couldn’t be prosecuted, but the film doesn’t seek to paint that wider picture. It instead remains nauseatingly focused on the base desires of the show’s creators and its fans, which it dramatizes through its radioactive texture. The film feels practically toxic, with characters who are entirely off-putting to watch, whether by way of Wever constantly popping her chewing gum, or a cameoing Creed Bratton (of The Office fame) appearing as a Hansen admirer turned on by fantasies of violence.

At the center of it all is Pattinson’s borderline sociopath. His Hansen is an animated, empty, Patrick Bateman-like vessel for celebrity allure, who remains the fulcrum of Oppenheim’s spinning, voyeuristic camera and its high-octane thrills. These are born not from guns and bombs, or even the stakes of catching a predator, but from the sheer exhilaration of seeing just how low Hansen and his cohorts will stoop to create entertainment, paving the path for the content-at-all-cost landscape in which we live today.

Thus begins an Earth-shattering cosmic battle between the God of Destruction and Goku and his allies—a conflict that will shake the entire universe.

articles.title: Zach Cregger Says He's Done With Franchise Films After Resident Evil
articles.summary: Resident Evil movie director Zach Cregger is days away from his survival horror adaptation's theatrical premiere, but don't expect to help bring another franchise film to the big screen ever again.
articles.body:
Resident Evil movie director Zach Cregger is days away from his survival horror adaptation's theatrical premiere, but don't expect to help bring another franchise film to the big screen ever again.

The filmmaker behind this month's Capcom project talked about what's next for him during a conversation with Deadline . When asked if he's ever been pressured to spearhead another recognizable IP, he gave a blunt answer: "I'm not doing that."

"I have never been approached by another franchise," Cregger said. "Maybe I have, but it would never get to me because I have been very clear that I’m not doing that. I’m doing this, and that’s it for me."

One might suspect Cregger's aversion to big franchise films like Resident Evil might stem from the backlash he's received in the months leading up to his movie's premiere. While the Barbarian and Weapons creator certainly has plenty of defenders looking forward to seeing his new live-action take, there have been many, many others who aren't quite as excited.

Most of the pressure has come from those who feel his Resident Evil doesn't align with the game it's based on. Changes to the source material, including its modern setting and snowy Raccoon City , have set fans on edge, while others aren't in love with the idea of following a new protagonist (Austin Abrams' Bryan Hodukavich) instead of someone like Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield.

The controversy surrounding the Resident Evil movie has been quite loud , but there are several factors at play when it comes to his plans for the future. He clarified that the decision comes down to his status as a writer who wants "to write whatever I want to write."

"I don’t want to write something where I have to make sure I'm tagging different data points to satisfy X," he continued. "I just want to satisfy me. And the only reason that I think Resident Evil is OK for me to do is because I’m enthusiastic about the games and I like the story that I thought of with the games and I’m making it for me. I think this movie is cool, and I hope it checks the fan boxes because I’m a fan and I’m checking my boxes.

"I'm making the Resident Evil movie that I wish existed, so I can do that with a clean heart and a clear conscience and not feel like I’m getting f**ked by some weird industry thing."

Cregger has made it abundantly clear that his Resident Evil movie is meant to be a love letter to the experience of playing games like Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 7 and not a direct retelling of any one particular story. Although he's writing off franchise films in the future, it sounds like another trip to Raccoon City – or maybe even somewhere else in the Resident Evil universe – isn't out of the question yet. In another recent interview, the director said he already has "ideas" for a sequel , even if we have yet to see how audiences will respond to the first movie.

Resident Evil is expected to have a big debut when it slithers into theaters September 18, 2026. Next up on his schedule are projects like the Siren Head movie , The Flood , and a Weapons prequel movie . While we wait to see Cregger's new vision for Raccoon City, you can check out a new trailer that revealed a sneak peek at a creature that looks suspiciously like RE4's Las Plagas . You can also check out its organ transplant bag-inspired popcorn bucket .
